shorts.title: They sold IBM. Then they sold Wal-Mart.
Why smart investors sell too early

beats.say: It's the early nineteen seventies. A big, successful fund management firm studies its own past mistakes. And it finds a painful one. Thirty years earlier, it had sold its IBM shares. If it had simply kept them, that one stake would have been bigger than all the money the firm now managed.

beats.say: So why did smart, rational investors keep selling? Sleep listed three reasons. Reason one. The wrong mental model. Most companies have one good idea, like a hit toy, and then struggle to repeat it. Sleep called this the Barbie problem. But Wal-Mart's engine didn't change from year to year.

beats.say: And here's the hidden trap. Investors know most companies fail, so they discount every stock for that risk. Even the ones that won't fail. That's how a great company's shares can stay cheap, in Sleep's words, in some cases, for decades.

beats.say: So, here's our verdict. The Wal-Mart moat was thrift, turned into lower prices, at ever growing scale, protected by a culture that never changed the formula. Its threat was a newer, cheaper scale sharer. And the lesson? It looked expensive for decades, and it was cheap the whole time.

beats.say: One. Has its engine, savings shared with customers, stayed the same for years? Two. Am I selling because a ratio looks high, or because the engine has stopped? Three. If I sell, will I track what I missed?
